\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
\label{sec:related-detection}

Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests on token-level distributions \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot approaches exploiting reference-model likelihoods \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers over linguistic features \cite{feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
Recent work has pursued diverse detection signals: \citet{intrinsic_dimension} use intrinsic dimensionality estimates, \citet{diveye} propose surprisal diversity features directly comparable to our distributional features, and \citet{generator_barrier} characterize the distributional gap between human and model outputs.
\citet{wu_survey_2025} provide the most comprehensive recent survey; see also \citet{jawahar_survey} for an earlier overview.
A persistent limitation is that all these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
Recent efforts extend detection to multi-class settings: \citet{beyond_binary} propose role recognition and involvement measurement to distinguish collaborative human-LLM generation scenarios, and the SemEval-2024 shared task \cite{semeval2024_task8} evaluates multi-generator attribution across domains and languages.
These approaches discriminate among different \emph{sources} (human vs.\ specific models) rather than recursive generation \emph{depth} within a single generator's chain.
Even when detection scores correlate with generation depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance when repurposed as ordinal predictors (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.71 across individual baselines; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), because each score captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently.
\citet{paraphrase_evades} and \citet{detection_possibilities} further demonstrate that detection robustness degrades under distributional shift.
Our reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores \cite{ood_baseline}; the contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the empirical finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.

\paragraph{Source attribution vs.\ depth estimation.}
A related but distinct task is \emph{source attribution}: identifying \emph{which} model generated a given text.
\citet{uchendu_attribution} train multi-class classifiers over stylometric features to distinguish outputs of different generators, and \citet{munir_looking_glass} learn attribution models that generalize across unseen language models.
These methods answer \emph{who} generated the text; depth estimation answers \emph{how many recursive steps} produced it.
The two tasks are orthogonal: a single generator can produce text at any depth, and texts at the same depth may originate from different generators.
Our LOGO evaluation explicitly decouples generator identity from depth by holding out entire generators, ensuring that the classifier learns depth signal rather than generator fingerprints.

\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
\label{sec:related-collapse}

A growing body of work studies quality degradation when models are trained on their own outputs.
\citet{self_consuming_mad} demonstrate that self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage, and \citet{curse_of_recursion} show that model collapse is inevitable in successive fine-tuning rounds without fresh human data, though \citet{model_collapse_avoidable} identify conditions under which careful data mixing can mitigate this effect.
\citet{strong_model_collapse} extend these results to larger-scale settings.
These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation, where model weights are updated on recursive data.
Our setting is different: we study \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.

Two concurrent lines of work are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss analogous to the telephone game.
\citet{markovian_chains} provide a theoretical framework for convergence in iterative text transformations, demonstrating that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics that bound distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
Our work differs in two respects: we study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal beyond the attractor bound; and we focus on \emph{estimating} depth from text features rather than characterizing convergence behavior.

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
\label{sec:related-diversity}

Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
Our surface features---type-token ratio and hapax ratio---instantiate this observation for inference chains, where we show monotonic diversity decline across generation depths without any model retraining.

These features are classical stylometric measures with a long history in authorship attribution \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship}.
\citet{uchendu_attribution} extend stylometric and neural methods to multi-class attribution of text to specific generators.
We push beyond generator identity to the \emph{depth} dimension: text from the same generator at different depths exhibits systematically different feature profiles, and these profiles generalize across generators.
Sampling strategies also affect diversity; \citet{nucleus_sampling} show that top-$p$ sampling mitigates some degeneration, but our results demonstrate that diversity still declines monotonically across recursive application of the same sampling procedure.

\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
\label{sec:related-provenance}

Scalable data curation relies on quality signals to filter web-crawled corpora.
\citet{dsir} select pretraining data to match a target distribution, \citet{qurating} learn quality scores from LLM judgments, and \citet{ccnet} filter Common Crawl via perplexity-based heuristics.
Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal: it characterizes \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source, orthogonal to content quality per se.

An alternative approach is proactive provenance through watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark}, where identifiable patterns are embedded during generation.
However, \citet{chainwash} demonstrate that watermark strength decays across multi-step generation chains, motivating passive post-hoc methods that do not require generator cooperation.
Our depth fingerprinting is such a method: it operates on text alone without assuming access to the generating model or an embedded watermark.
At the feature level, our reference-model NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability distribution's lower tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for a different purpose---ordinal depth estimation rather than training-set membership.

2. 是否设置了 `enable_thinking=False`（关闭 thinking mode 做纯 generation）
3. 模型名**不含** "-Base" 后缀即为 instruct 版本

1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
5	
6	\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
7	\label{sec:results-classification}
8	
9	Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.
10	
11	The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.789 (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), the gen-0 class F1 (0.94) may be inflated; we therefore report a leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, F1\,=\,0.723) as the primary metric in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}.
12	Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
13	Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.
14	
15	\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
16	The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
17	However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
18	Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
19	Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+1.1\,pp to 0.811), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.
20	A volume-matched control confirms this gain is driven by generator diversity, not data quantity: upsampling the 4-generator training set to match the 5-generator count yields only +0.05\,pp, while the remaining +0.78\,pp (94\% of the total improvement) is attributable to the additional generator's distributional diversity.
21	We note that this gap may narrow with scale-matched training data; our current dataset contains $\sim$1{,}000 samples per generator regardless of scale.
22	
23	\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
24	Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).
25	
26	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
27	Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
28	Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).
29	
30	
31	\begin{table}[t]
32	\centering
33	\small
34	\begin{tabular}{llccc}
35	\toprule
36	\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Held-out F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
37	\midrule
38	Pythia-1B       & Pythia & 1.0B & 0.856 & [0.843, 0.863] \\
39	Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia & 2.8B & 0.804 & [0.793, 0.813] \\
40	OLMo-2-1B      & OLMo   & 1.5B & 0.764 & [0.754, 0.776] \\
41	Qwen3-0.6B     & Qwen   & 0.6B & 0.824 & [0.813, 0.834] \\
42	Qwen3-1.7B     & Qwen   & 1.7B & 0.806 & [0.796, 0.817] \\
43	Qwen3-8B       & Qwen   & 8.2B & 0.683 & [0.668, 0.694] \\
44	\midrule
45	\multicolumn{3}{l}{Average (6-gen LOGO)} & 0.789 & --- \\
46	\multicolumn{3}{l}{5-gen LOGO (excl.\ Qwen3-8B)} & 0.800 & --- \\
47	\bottomrule
48	\end{tabular}
49	\caption{Leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals ($n$\,=\,1000) for 3-class depth estimation using the 7-feature ensemble. Each row holds out one generator for testing and trains on the remaining five.}
50	\label{tab:logo-results}
51	\end{table}
52	
53	\paragraph{Ordinal regression comparison.}
54	To test whether the ordinal structure of the 3-class depth label provides additional discriminative power, we compare CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral_ordinal} and Frank-Hall ordinal reduction \cite{frank_hall_ordinal} against the standard multiclass XGBoost classifier under the same LOGO protocol.
55	On 3-class F1, CORAL achieves 0.771, Frank-Hall 0.793, and XGBoost 0.789; all three confidence intervals overlap.
56	Binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) similarly shows no separation: XGBoost 0.721, CORAL 0.728.
57	Concordance index---an ordinal-specific metric rewarding correct ranking---yields XGBoost 0.821, CORAL 0.810, Frank-Hall 0.825; again, all CIs overlap.
58	The standard multiclass classifier already captures the depth-discriminative signal, and explicitly encoding ordinal structure does not yield a measurable gain, likely because the 3-class granularity provides insufficient ordinal resolution for ranking-aware losses to exploit.
59	
60	
61	\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
62	\label{sec:results-differential}
63	
64	Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
65	This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).
66	
67	\begin{figure}[t]
68	\centering
69	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
70	\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Central-tendency and diversity features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show strong monotonic drift, while shape features (entropy std, tail decay) remain near-stationary.}
71	\label{fig:feature-drift}
72	\end{figure}
73	
74	Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
75	drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),
76	while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.089$).
77	
78	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
79	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
80	The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.789) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR, hapax\_ratio; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy mean/std/max/min, tail\_decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
81	Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.269), followed by entropy mean (0.164) and TTR (0.159).
82	Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.
83	
84	\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
85	To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
86	All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
87	The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.
88	
89	
90	\begin{table}[t]
91	\centering
92	\small
93	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
94	\toprule
95	\textbf{Feature set} & \textbf{LOGO F1} & \textbf{Top feature (importance)} \\
96	\midrule
97	Full (7 features)     & 0.789 & hapax\_ratio (0.269) \\
98	Surface only (2)      & 0.729 & hapax\_ratio (0.320) \\
99	Reference only (5)    & 0.745 & entropy\_mean (0.218) \\
100	\bottomrule
101	\end{tabular}
102	\caption{Feature ablation (6-gen LOGO). Full $>$ surface = reference confirms complementarity between surface diversity features and reference-model distributional features.}
103	\label{tab:ablation}
104	\end{table}
105	
106	Leave-one-feature-out analysis confirms that 6 of 7 features contribute positively, with entropy\_max showing the largest marginal impact despite modest split frequency (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).
107

109	\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
110	\label{sec:results-baselines}
111	
112	\begin{figure}[t]
113	\centering
114	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_baseline_comparison.png}
115	\caption{LOGO macro-F1 with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals for each detection baseline and the 7-feature ensemble. Per-generator held-out F1 varies more for single detectors than for the ensemble.}
116	\label{fig:baseline-ci}
117	\end{figure}
118	
119	We repurpose four existing detection scores as ordinal depth predictors by training the same classifier on each score as a single feature, using identical LOGO evaluation.
120	Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), 3-class LOGO evaluation creates a train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
121	We therefore report both 3-class and binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) results; the binary metric is the primary measure of depth discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).
122	
123	\begin{table}[t]
124	\centering
125	\small
126	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
127	\toprule
128	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{Per-gen std} \\
129	\midrule
130	7-feature ensemble    & 0.789 & \textbf{0.723} & 0.051 \\
131	4-det.\ + surface     & \textbf{0.805} & 0.724 & 0.049 \\
132	4-detector ens.\      & 0.796 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
133	Avg-LogProb           & 0.737 & 0.712 & 0.044 \\
134	LD-Score              & 0.655 & 0.701 & 0.045 \\
135	FastDetectGPT         & 0.688 & 0.616 & 0.056 \\
136	Binoculars            & 0.417 & 0.524 & 0.022 \\
137	\bottomrule
138	\end{tabular}
139	\caption{Depth classification under unified 6-gen LOGO evaluation. \textbf{3-class}: gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+ (gen-0 samples shared across generators; see \S\ref{sec:generation}). \textbf{Binary}: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ only, eliminating the gen-0 train--test overlap. Per-gen std measures cross-generator consistency of the binary metric. The 7-feature ensemble is the strongest single-model method on both metrics and matches the best multi-detector ensemble on binary F1.}
140	\label{tab:baselines}
141	\end{table}
142	
143	The 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723, outperforming every individual detection baseline: +1.1\,pp over Avg-LogProb, +2.2\,pp over LD-Score, +10.7\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +19.9\,pp over Binoculars ($p < 0.001$ for all comparisons).
144	On the 3-class metric, the ensemble (0.789) similarly outperforms all single baselines, though the margins are inflated by the gen-0 overlap.
145	
146	\paragraph{Multi-detector ensembles.}
147	Combining all four detection scores into a 4-detector ensemble yields binary F1\,=\,0.712---below the 7-feature ensemble (0.723).
148	The multi-detector advantage seen in 3-class evaluation (0.796 vs.\ 0.789) is driven entirely by superior gen-0 classification; existing detectors excel at human-vs-machine discrimination but do not capture the finer depth signal between gen-1 and gen-2+.
149	Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble raises binary F1 to 0.724, matching the 7-feature ensemble and confirming that surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
150	Baseline results are stable across classifier hyperparameters: using the ensemble's settings ($n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$) instead of the default ($100$/$3$) changes baseline F1 by less than 0.002\,pp, confirming that performance differences reflect feature informativeness rather than classifier capacity.
151	
152	\paragraph{Binoculars: a non-transferable signal.}
153	Binoculars achieves near-random performance on the depth task (3-class F1\,=\,0.417, binary F1\,=\,0.524), confirming that cross-model perplexity ratios---the core signal in Binoculars---do not transfer to depth discrimination.
154	
155	
156	\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}
157	\label{sec:results-downstream}
158	
159	Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
160	We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).
161	
162	\begin{table}[t]
163	\centering
164	\small
165	\begin{tabular}{lrc}
166	\toprule
167	\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
168	\midrule
169	All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
170	Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
171	Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
172	Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
173	Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
174	\bottomrule
175	\end{tabular}
176	\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
177	\label{tab:downstream}
178	\end{table}
179	
180	The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
181	Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
182	At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
183	Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.
184	
185	Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.
186	
187	We report this negative finding transparently: depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data curation.
188	Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
5	Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
6	One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
7	Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
8	If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
9	We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.
10	
11	\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
12	Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
13	Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
14	This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
15	Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.
16	
17	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
18	The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
19	Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
20	Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
21	Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
22	Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.
23	
24	\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
25	Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
26	This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
27	The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.
28	
29	\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
30	Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
31	Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
32	We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
33	This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
34	The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.
35	
36	\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
37	Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
38	However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
39	Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
40	Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
41	The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.
42	
43	\paragraph{Depth features vs.\ multi-detector ensembles.}
44	In 3-class evaluation, multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 (0.805 with surface features added vs.\ 0.789).
45	However, this advantage is driven entirely by gen-0 classification, where detection scores excel at human-vs-machine discrimination.
46	In the leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), the 7-feature ensemble matches the best multi-detector configuration (0.723 vs.\ 0.724), demonstrating that depth features capture the gen-1/gen-2+ distinction as effectively as four detection pipelines combined.
47	Depth features additionally offer interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern---and computational efficiency, requiring only a single lightweight reference model.
48	
49	\paragraph{Same-family reference bias.}
50	Pythia-1B achieves the highest held-out F1 (0.856) despite using a same-family reference model (Pythia-410M).
51	Cross-family references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) yield nearly identical Pythia-1B F1 (0.845--0.848), confirming that this generator's high detectability reflects its intrinsic generation patterns rather than reference-model family bias.
52	
53	\paragraph{Instruct tuning degrades depth signal through multiple mechanisms.}
54	Preliminary experiments with instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 for base OLMo-2-1B), and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template yields F1\,=\,0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 for the base model).
55	Length-controlled analysis reveals that this degradation is multi-faceted.
56	Surface-level features (TTR, hapax ratio) are largely confounded by length collapse: both instruct models produce outputs with strongly negative length--depth correlations (OLMo-Instruct $\rho = -0.370$; Qwen3 chat $\rho = -0.583$), and once output length is partialled out, surface feature--depth associations weaken or reverse.
57	By contrast, entropy-based features exhibit genuine behavioral shifts that survive length control.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.

\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.

\paragraph{Depth features vs.\ multi-detector ensembles.}
In 3-class evaluation, multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 (0.805 with surface features added vs.\ 0.789).
However, this advantage is driven entirely by gen-0 classification, where detection scores excel at human-vs-machine discrimination.
In the leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), the 7-feature ensemble matches the best multi-detector configuration (0.723 vs.\ 0.724), demonstrating that depth features capture the gen-1/gen-2+ distinction as effectively as four detection pipelines combined.
Depth features additionally offer interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern---and computational efficiency, requiring only a single lightweight reference model.

\paragraph{Same-family reference bias.}
Pythia-1B achieves the highest held-out F1 (0.856) despite using a same-family reference model (Pythia-410M).
Cross-family references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) yield nearly identical Pythia-1B F1 (0.845--0.848), confirming that this generator's high detectability reflects its intrinsic generation patterns rather than reference-model family bias.

\paragraph{Instruct tuning degrades depth signal through multiple mechanisms.}
Preliminary experiments with instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 for base OLMo-2-1B), and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template yields F1\,=\,0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 for the base model).
Length-controlled analysis reveals that this degradation is multi-faceted.
Surface-level features (TTR, hapax ratio) are largely confounded by length collapse: both instruct models produce outputs with strongly negative length--depth correlations (OLMo-Instruct $\rho = -0.370$; Qwen3 chat $\rho = -0.583$), and once output length is partialled out, surface feature--depth associations weaken or reverse.
By contrast, entropy-based features exhibit genuine behavioral shifts that survive length control.
OLMo-Instruct retains a moderate entropy--depth partial correlation ($\rho = 0.364$ after controlling for length), suggesting that instruction tuning alters the entropy dynamics of recursive generation beyond what length differences explain.
Qwen3 chat shows a weaker residual ($\rho = 0.161$), indicating that the extent of genuine depth-signal preservation varies across model families.
These preliminary observations---based on two instruct models---suggest that instruction tuning disrupts depth fingerprints through a combination of length homogenization (which confounds surface features) and altered generation dynamics (which affect entropy features independently of length).
Disentangling these mechanisms across a broader set of instruct models is a priority for future work; the current findings justify restricting our scope to base models where length confounds are minimal.

\paragraph{Instruct tuning degrades depth signal through multiple mechanisms.}
Preliminary experiments with instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 for base OLMo-2-1B), and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template yields F1\,=\,0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 for the base model).
Length-controlled analysis reveals two distinct patterns.
Entropy-based features consistently reverse sign across all three instruct models (partial $\rho$ = +0.103, +0.161, +0.364 for Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, and OLMo-Instruct respectively), suggesting a genuine shift in the generation process that survives length control.
In contrast, surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) show model-dependent behavior: Qwen models retain weakly positive partial correlations with depth (TTR partial $\rho$ = +0.139, +0.130; hapax partial $\rho$ = +0.125, +0.166 for Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B), while OLMo-Instruct exhibits negative correlations similar to base models (TTR partial $\rho = -0.241$; hapax partial $\rho = -0.198$).
This divergence cautions against treating surface feature reversal as a universal consequence of instruction tuning; the effect is architecture- or training-recipe-dependent.

OLMo-Instruct presents a paradox: it exhibits the strongest entropy--depth partial correlation (+0.364) yet the worst classification performance (LOGO F1\,=\,0.338).
A likely explanation is that its surface features retain base-model polarity (negative partial $\rho$) while entropy reverses to positive, creating contradictory signals for a classifier trained on base-model patterns---where entropy and surface features are jointly negative at greater depths.
OLMo-Instruct breaks this joint structure, and the resulting signal conflict may account for the classification collapse.
Disentangling these mechanisms across a broader set of instruct models is a priority for future work; the current findings justify restricting our scope to base models where such confounds are minimal.
